## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{100}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a large archive of successful demonstrations leave a robot unable to recover from its first mistake?_

A successful demonstration shows how one machine completed a task under one set of conditions. It shows almost nothing about what to do after a slip, a shifted fixture, or a worn gripper, yet a learned policy's first error carries it into exactly those states, where the archive holds no instruction. Repeating the demonstration enlarges the archive without filling that gap. The recorded motion also carries the operator's delay, the machine's limits, and every correction the permission path applied, so a training process that cannot separate these influences learns a safeguard's intervention or a mechanical limitation as if it were skill. Gathering the missing experience costs operator time and component life, and the collection itself must stay within the machine's physical limits. Physical data must therefore be engineered, from the choice of experiences to the meaning, timing, and physical origin of every label and the conditions the archive leaves uncovered. Because every collected action crosses the causal boundary, its irreversible costs decide what a machine can learn and where its evidence stops.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Analyze the conditional quadratic imitation-cost bound and distinguish dataset occupancy from evaluated closed-loop competence
- Select the action tap a dataset imitates and align multi-rate sensor and action streams to hardware exposure-midpoint timestamps within the task's spatial tolerance
- Estimate usable demonstration yield from collection time, operator rest, and physical reset overhead, and budget the mechanical component wear a campaign consumes
- Identify collection gaps by joining empirical state-action occupancy against a required scenario ledger
- Separate failed autonomous actions from admissible human recovery across the divergence, takeover, and stabilization timestamps of an intervention episode
- Evaluate whether an embodiment's mechanical, sensing, and timing assumptions transfer to another machine without falling into the normalization fallacy
- Detect silent calibration and plant drift in a demonstration archive using kinematic reprojection and repeated excitation trajectories
- Design an immutable provenance record linking each observation to its four-stream action taps ($\RequestedActionTap, \MappedCommandTap, \EnforcedCommandTap, \MeasuredResponseTap$) and to the collecting plant

:::

## Endogenous Experience {#sec-data-endogenous-experience}

In most machine learning, the dataset exists before the engineering begins. A text corpus or an image benchmark is gathered independently of the model, costs little per additional example, and does not change in response to anything the model predicts. A physical machine has no such corpus. Collecting demonstrations on the robot consumes operator time and component life; robot-free and synthetic sources avoid that robot wear but still require qualification for the target machine. Every telemetry record reflects who commanded the action, what the permission path admitted, and how the physical body moved. Furthermore, each executed action changes the physical state of the system, dictating what subsequent observations can reveal. Physical data is therefore an engineered artifact. The central challenge of physical data engineering is deciding which experiences to collect, and what to record about them, so that a policy learns the task rather than the idiosyncrasies of its collection. Answering this challenge requires four elements: accounting for collection costs in operator time and hardware wear, defining an unambiguous meaning for every recorded action label, establishing a metric for state-space coverage independent of the archive's internal contents, and explicitly auditing what the archive omits.

Consider a warehouse mobile manipulator tasked with opening a spring-latched cage door: the robot can flawlessly enforce its low-level motion limits and yet fail because it lacks the operational experience to unlatch the door. During a demonstration, a human operator commands motion, the safety permission path checks and filters it, and the robot's physical body drives against the mechanical latch. The onboard sensor log captures the output of that entire coupled loop. The limits and handoffs that Part I recorded for this machine, in the limit record of @sec-body-limit-record-schema and the handoff record of @sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix, therefore become preconditions on the training data fed to the learned policy proposer, since every logged command was shaped by them before the body moved. Choosing which physical experiences to collect demands a rigorous accounting of how control inputs shift future sensory states; choosing what to imitate requires cleanly separating the operator's raw request from the safety-filtered command and the measured physical response.

A policy fit by supervised imitation to nominal, clean teleoperated demonstrations of door openings (behavioral cloning, defined below) can execute flawlessly in simulation yet jam the latch during its first autonomous deployment. The primary culprit is the distribution shift that the machine's own closed-loop actions induce. Unlike passive inference on a fixed benchmark, an action executed within an embodied Markov decision process (MDP), in which the next state depends on the current state and action, physically alters the robot's spatial trajectory, camera viewpoint, and contact states. That displacement changes the probability distribution of every subsequent sensory observation ($\DecisionProcessState_{t+1} \sim \EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\DecisionProcessState \mid \DecisionProcessState_{t}, \CognitivePolicyAction_{t})$).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The Markov decision process, with its transition model and reward, is developed for the latch task in @sec-training-rl-primer.
:::

::: {#dfn-data-endogenous-covariate-shift .callout-definition title="Endogenous covariate shift"}

***Endogenous covariate shift***\index{Endogenous covariate shift!definition}\index{Covariate drift!physical AI} is the closed-loop distribution discrepancy wherein an embodied agent's executed actions alter its subsequent physical states and sensory observations ($\DecisionProcessState_{t+1} \sim \EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\DecisionProcessState \mid \DecisionProcessState_{t}, \CognitivePolicyAction_{t})$), driving the system into state-space regimes unsupported by its training demonstrations.

1.  **Significance**: Explains how offline behavioral cloning can fail during closed-loop physical execution: a perturbation may drive the system into states where the policy lacks training support.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike exogenous dataset shift caused by changing ambient lighting or seasonal weather, endogenous shift is actively generated by the agent's own closed-loop actions altering its subsequent observation distribution.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Attempting to fix closed-loop policy failure by collecting more nominal expert demonstrations, which only increases data density along the success manifold without providing the corrective recovery data needed to escape boundary excursions.

:::

This distribution shift is how the second law, endogenous data (principle \ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}), shows up in data collection, where the machine's own actions choose the states its archive must later answer for. An archive composed exclusively of flawless executions without recovery trajectories becomes an operational liability: the moment the autonomous policy commits its first sub-millimeter tracking error, the robot enters states never encountered during training.

### Mechanics of endogenous covariate shift {#sec-data-covariate-shift}

In classical statistical learning theory, empirical risk minimization assumes that samples are drawn independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) from an exogenous, stationary distribution $\ExogenousDataDistribution$. An image classifier that misidentifies a dog as a cat does not alter the pixels of subsequent images in the test set. The covariate shift encountered in imitation learning is the closed-loop, endogenous counterpart to this setting. Passive machine learning uses the term *covariate shift* to describe an open-loop observational phenomenon: the marginal input distribution $\InputDistribution$ changes (such as evaluating a vision model trained on sunny daytime driving under rainy nighttime illumination) while the underlying conditional data-generating function $\ConditionalDistribution$ remains stationary. In that setting, the model remains a passive observer: its predictions $\PassiveModelPrediction$ exert zero physical back-action on the environment, and an inference error does not physically mutate subsequent inputs.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The closed loop through which a flawed proposal carries the machine into states missing from its training distribution is established in @sec-boundary-tensors-to-silicon.
:::

In an embodied physical system, two distinct mechanisms distort what the learner encounters. The first mechanism shifts the states that the policy visits even when the underlying hardware remains unchanged; the second mechanism actively alters how the physical plant responds to any given control input:

1. **Endogenous state distribution shift**: The policy's executed actions $\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} = \Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t})$ directly drive the physical state transition $\DecisionProcessState_{t+1} \sim \EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\DecisionProcessState \mid \DecisionProcessState_{t}, \CognitivePolicyAction_{t})$, actively determining the sensory observations $\MultimodalObservation_{t+1}$ the robot encounters next. A single control error displaces the physical body into an unvisited region of the state space, immediately mutating the incoming observation distribution.
2. **Active physical plant drift**: The physical plant is a continuous dynamical system governed by differential equations of motion $\PlantStateRate = \PlantDynamicsFunction(\MechanicalPlantState, \ControlInput; \PlantDynamicsParameters(\TimeInstant))$ whose parameters actively drift over operational time. Actuator Joule heating ($\TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \ElectricalResistance(\WindingTemperature)$) elevates winding temperature and increases copper resistance via $\ElectricalResistance(\WindingTemperature) = \ElectricalResistance_0(1 + \CopperTemperatureCoefficient \JouleanTemperatureRise)$. This resistance rise compresses the motor drive's available voltage headroom, capping the electrical current and peak torque delivered at high joint velocities. Over extended operating cycles, continuous loading degrades strain-wave gearbox lubrication, lowering torsional stiffness and expanding mechanical lost motion. Similarly, compliant elastomer gripper pads wear down and deform, shrinking the Coulomb friction cone ($\lVert \TangentialContactShear \rVert \le \CoulombFrictionCoefficient \NormalContactForce$). Finally, physical workpieces exhibit unmodeled variations in mass, center of gravity, and surface texture across trials, perturbing both the inertial loads the arm must accelerate and the gravitational torques the joints must sustain.

In embodied control, the policy's closed-loop actions induce an *endogenous state visitation distribution* $\LearnerStateVisitationDistribution(\DecisionProcessState)$, defined as the expected fraction of time steps that a rollout of policy $\pi$ spends in state $\DecisionProcessState$. When an agent is trained via offline behavioral cloning on demonstrations generated by an expert policy $\pi^*$, empirical risk minimization optimizes the imitation objective strictly over the expert's occupancy distribution $\ExpertStateVisitationDistribution(\DecisionProcessState)$. During autonomous execution, however, the learned policy must generate control actions under its own induced distribution $\LearnerStateVisitationDistribution(\DecisionProcessState)$. Any divergence between $\ExpertStateVisitationDistribution$ and $\LearnerStateVisitationDistribution$ can trigger cascading execution errors whenever the policy encounters a state lacking demonstrated corrective actions.

::: {#dfn-data-behavioral-cloning .callout-definition title="Behavioral cloning"}

***Behavioral cloning***\index{Behavioral cloning!definition} is imitation learning posed as supervised learning: a policy is fit to map each recorded observation to the action the demonstrator took there, with the loss weighted by the demonstrator's own state occupancy $\ExpertStateVisitationDistribution$.

1.  **Significance**: Training error is measured only on states the demonstrator visited, while deployment cost accrues on the states the learned policy visits. Under a 0–1 action loss (one whenever the policy's action differs from the expert's, zero otherwise) the worst-case excess cost can therefore grow with the square of the horizon $\BehaviorCloningHorizon$, the episode length in control steps, rather than linearly, as the next subsection derives.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike corrective aggregation, which obtains expert labels at states the learner itself reaches (@sec-data-intervention-recovery develops it), behavioral cloning never observes the consequences of its own mistakes; unlike reinforcement learning, it needs demonstrations but no reward.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Reading a low held-out loss as evidence of closed-loop competence. A held-out split drawn from the same demonstrations shares their occupancy, so it cannot contain the states the policy's first error reaches.

:::

### Recovery and compounding error {#sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability}

Opening a latch from a nominal centered approach and recovering from an off-axis sideways slip require different physical actions (@fig-05-latch-corridor). Every retained demonstration guides the gripper forward along the narrow corridor centered on the strike plate, populating the archive with thousands of forward-progress actions. The archive contains zero demonstrations starting from a gripper displaced a few millimeters toward the fixture that return it to the centerline. A skilled human operator rarely permits the gripper to drift into those boundary regimes, and teleoperation runs that exhibited noticeable drift were routinely aborted or discarded during curation.[^fn-alvinn-recovery-latch] At such a displaced state, nothing in the training data constrains the policy's output. The **recoverability problem**\index{Recoverability problem} is precisely this absence of demonstrated corrective actions directing the system back into the nominal corridor.

[^fn-alvinn-recovery-latch]: **ALVINN (Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network)**\index{ALVINN!recovery data}: Pomerleau's road-following network learned to steer from a human driver who kept the van centered, so its training images held almost no off-center views [@pomerleau1989alvinn]. His remedy shifted each camera image sideways in software and corrected the steering label to match, synthesizing recovery examples about 20 years before Dataset Aggregation (DAgger, @sec-data-intervention-recovery) [@pomerleau1991efficient]. A warp could fill that gap because the missing state was only a viewpoint of a flat road, whereas a gripper displaced toward the fixture also lacks contact forces that no image transform can manufacture, so its recoveries must be demonstrated or collected.

::: {#fig-05-latch-corridor fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The latch corridor seen from above**: Retained demonstrations supply dense forward-progress actions inside a narrow corridor centered on the strike plate. A gripper displaced toward the fixture sits where the archive holds no demonstration, so nothing in the data specifies the action that returns it to the corridor, and an unconstrained output can carry it farther toward contact." fig-alt="Top-view sketch. A shaded horizontal corridor runs left to right toward a strike plate on the right, with five arrows pointing along its centerline. Above the corridor, a small square marks a displaced gripper. A dashed arrow from the gripper toward the corridor is labeled as the missing return action, and a dashed arrow from the gripper toward a shaded fixture band at the top is labeled as drift into contact."}
![](images/svg/fig05_latch_corridor.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Whether this missing return action leads to task failure depends on the closed-loop dynamics of the complete physical plant. Because the robot's physical state encompasses joint coordinates, joint velocities, motor drive currents, contact wrenches (combined three-axis contact forces and torques), and raw camera streams, a nominal demonstration traces an infinitesimally thin manifold through a high-dimensional state space. Almost any unmodeled disturbance displaces the system off this path. If the physical plant and its low-level joint controllers inherently restore small lateral displacements toward the centerline through compliant passive dynamics, an imperfect policy output near the corridor boundary will naturally attenuate. If the system dynamics lack this self-centering stability, the tracking error will persist or compound until a learned recovery policy, the safety permission path, or a human supervisor intervenes. While production demonstration archives often contain occasional human corrections, their coverage cannot be assumed; it must be audited against an explicit scenario ledger (@sec-data-policy-coverage).

The quadratic worst-case scaling of behavioral cloning can be derived through a discrete summation over horizon steps. Suppose an autonomous agent follows the expert trajectory until encountering its first execution error at step $\FirstErrorStepIndex \in \{1, \dots, \BehaviorCloningHorizon\}$. If this error propels the system into an unsupported state from which it never recovers, the agent incurs an adverse task cost at every remaining step ($\BehaviorCloningHorizon - \FirstErrorStepIndex$). Assigning each time step an upper bound $\SingleStepImitationError$ on the probability of committing a first error and normalizing the per-step cost to unity ($\ImmediateTaskCostScore_t = 1$) yields the following worst-case cost accumulation. This discrete summation serves as an upper-bound derivation rather than an exact expectation over independent failure events:
$$\sum_{\FirstErrorStepIndex=1}^\BehaviorCloningHorizon \SingleStepImitationError (\BehaviorCloningHorizon - \FirstErrorStepIndex) = \SingleStepImitationError \left( \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2 - \sum_{\FirstErrorStepIndex=1}^\BehaviorCloningHorizon \FirstErrorStepIndex \right) = \SingleStepImitationError \left( \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2 - \frac{\BehaviorCloningHorizon(\BehaviorCloningHorizon+1)}{2} \right) = \frac{\BehaviorCloningHorizon(\BehaviorCloningHorizon-1)}{2} \SingleStepImitationError \approx \frac{1}{2} \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2 \SingleStepImitationError.$$
Contrast this result with open-loop supervised learning: if per-step inference errors were independent and exerted zero feedback on subsequent model inputs, an error rate of $\SingleStepImitationError$ per step would scale linearly over $\BehaviorCloningHorizon$ steps as $\sum_{t=1}^\BehaviorCloningHorizon \SingleStepImitationError = \BehaviorCloningHorizon\SingleStepImitationError$. The extra factor of $\BehaviorCloningHorizon$ appearing in $\CovariateDriftBound$ is the mathematical signature of closed-loop endogenous feedback.

This quadratic bound characterizes the accumulation of task cost over time, not the physical trajectory of the machine. The result does not imply that spatial tracking errors grow quadratically as $\TimeInstant^2$. Closed-loop contact forces, mechanical compliance, and actuator saturation govern how physical trajectories evolve; the derivation formalizes only the cost of operating in states where the policy lacks training support.

Formally, let $\pi$ represent the learned policy, $\pi^*$ the expert demonstration policy, $\ExpectedTaskCostSum$ the expected cumulative task cost over horizon $\BehaviorCloningHorizon$, and $\SingleStepImitationError$ the upper bound on the probability of action disagreement across expert-visited states under a 0–1 action loss: $\mathbb{E}_{\DecisionProcessState \sim \ExpertStateVisitationDistribution} [\IndicatorFunction(\pi(\DecisionProcessState) \ne \pi^*(\DecisionProcessState))] \le \SingleStepImitationError$. Assuming per-step task costs lie in $[0,1]$, behavioral cloning\index{Behavioral cloning!quadratic error compounding} admits the worst-case bound (@eq-data-quadratic-drift) derived by @ross2010efficient and restated by @ross2011reduction:
$$\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)-\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi^*) \le \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2\SingleStepImitationError.$$ {#eq-data-quadratic-drift}
The published theorem carries a constant of one rather than the sketch's one half; both are worst-case bounds, and their quadratic dependence on the horizon is the same.

In practice, this theoretical bound can exceed the maximum possible cost achievable in a finite episode. Because per-step costs are bounded in $[0,1]$, the excess cost is trivially bounded by $\BehaviorCloningHorizon$; hence, $\min(\BehaviorCloningHorizon, \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2\SingleStepImitationError)$ represents the operational upper bound. Once the quadratic expression surpasses $\BehaviorCloningHorizon$, it provides no meaningful prediction regarding physical failure rates or contact severity. The practical engineering value of this bound lies in exposing why behavioral cloning has no defense in states its demonstrations never reached, rather than in predicting exact physical collision rates.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The full derivation of the quadratic bound, with its loss and cost assumptions, is developed in @sec-appendix-ml-compounding.
:::

The actual scaling with horizon length depends heavily on the chosen loss function, the action space, and the closed-loop plant stability; consequently, @eq-data-quadratic-drift reflects a classical result for discrete 0–1 loss rather than an absolute law for all imitation architectures. When trained under logarithmic loss (minimizing the negative log-probability assigned to expert actions) over a well-specified policy class containing the expert, behavioral cloning can achieve a sample complexity that does not grow with the horizon length, provided total reward is bounded and the policy class capacity is controlled [@foster2024behavior]. Continuous action spaces, however, introduce the opposite challenge. Even when the physical closed loop is exponentially stable (small mechanical perturbations decay at a fixed rate) and the expert policy is smooth and deterministic, any smooth, deterministic imitator can exhibit closed-loop execution errors that scale exponentially with horizon length relative to its training loss [@simchowitz2025pitfalls]. The same analysis identifies two ways around this compounding [@simchowitz2025pitfalls]. The first changes the policy class: a policy that is non-smooth, that is non-Markovian (its action depends on the recent history and not only the current observation), or whose action distribution is multimodal (it can place probability on several distinct actions at once, rather than averaging them) escapes the result, and action chunking and diffusion decoders have these properties. The second changes the data: demonstrations deliberately spread across a wide tube surrounding the nominal trajectory. That second remedy is a data-collection decision, and @sec-data-intervention-recovery returns to it as noise injection during teleoperation. Because the mobile manipulator operates in a continuous control space, closed-loop success ultimately hinges on whether the combined policy and low-level controllers actively restore a displaced gripper to the nominal path.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Action chunking, in which the policy emits a short sequence of setpoints per inference, is established in @sec-brain-action-chunking.
:::

Collecting more nominal expert demonstrations does not resolve endogenous covariate shift. Adding another thousand hours of clean, centered door openings merely increases sample density along the nominal trajectory; the empirical support outside this narrow tube remains strictly zero ($\ExpertStateVisitationDistribution(\DecisionProcessState) = 0$). This pitfall is the *nominal demonstration trap*. Furthermore, logging physical robot experience carries direct hardware costs. While a web crawler scrapes static text with zero marginal mechanical wear, every recorded second of robot telemetry consumes actuator fatigue life, heats motor windings ($d\WindingTemperature/d\TimeInstant$), wears down gearbox teeth, and depletes battery reserves. In practical data-collection campaigns, required pauses for operator fatigue, sensor recalibration, scene resets, and discarded trials often leave less than one quarter of scheduled workcell time as usable demonstration data (@sec-data-teleop-costs). Physical telemetry is scarce, wear-intensive, and costly; collecting it without modeling closed-loop recovery dynamics compromises policy training.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Actuator thermal dissipation ($d\WindingTemperature/d\TimeInstant$) and winding damage limits are established in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.
:::

A physical command also undergoes substantial semantic shifts as it traverses the control stack toward the actuators. In a system partitioned by the proposal boundary, an operator's or policy's requested action is mapped into a trajectory setpoint, evaluated and potentially modified by the safety permission path, and executed by the physical plant to produce a measured response. Logging only the raw requested action trains the policy on commands the plant may be physically incapable of realizing. Conversely, logging only the measured plant response teaches the policy to reproduce structural deflection, link flexure, and gear backlash as though they represented intentional human control skill.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The proposal boundary, which separates a learned proposer from the permission path that alone may admit an action, is established in @sec-boundary-machine-model.
:::

A physical data-collection campaign must therefore resolve two architectural decisions before recording its first trajectory: which controller source dictates the actions, and which of these four representations of one command (the request, the mapped setpoint, the admitted command, and the measured response) the dataset will preserve as its training label.

## Physical Telemetry Sources and Ingestion Modalities {#sec-data-collection-sources}

Manipulating a mechanism such as a warehouse cage-door latch reveals how heavily the telemetry source shapes the resulting dataset. An engineer can physically guide the robot arm, command it through a remote teleoperation rig, or dispatch an automated controller to execute the trajectory. Each ingestion path fundamentally alters which tracking errors, recovery maneuvers, and transient contacts reach the archive. Because collection on the robot consumes machine operating hours, joint wear, and human engineering effort, selecting a telemetry source represents an architectural trade-off between operational cost and the useful experience yielded per attempted episode.

In a streaming telemetry architecture, physical data sources separate according to who chooses the action and how the control stream enters the ingestion pipeline:

1. In **kinesthetic teaching**, a colocated human demonstrator physically grasps and guides the unpowered or gravity-compensated links of the mechanism. The logging pipeline records joint encoder positions at the native controller rate without network transport delays. However, human biomechanics govern the motion's bandwidth, moving far more slowly than the controller's sampling loop, while labor costs scale $1:1$ with demonstrator time. Furthermore, the demonstrator's body frequently occludes onboard camera views, introducing systematic visual distribution shifts relative to autonomous operation.
2. In **teleoperation**, a remote operator manipulates an input device to puppet the follower robot across a network fabric.[^fn-goertz-force-teleop] Teleoperation interfaces differ in how operator inputs map to robot actuators and how much physical contact information reflects back to the human. Joint-space leader-follower arms such as ALOHA [@zhao2023learning] and GELLO [@wu2023gello] mirror the follower's joint topology, often at reduced scale, streaming joint angles directly to the follower without inverse kinematics (computing the joint angles that place the tool at a commanded pose). In contrast, tracked spatial controllers and rate-controlled space mice command Cartesian tool poses or velocities that require inverse kinematics solvers at runtime, while force-reflecting bilateral arms actively transmit measured contact forces back to the operator's hands. @Tbl-05-teleop-taxonomy compares these interfaces and names the artifact each leaves in the recording.
3. In **scripted collection**, a deterministic trajectory generator executes automated motion primitives, such as cubic splines or impedance-governed state machines. Ingestion rates are high and predictable ($50\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$), but trajectories traverse rigid, repetitive manifolds. Because these paths fail to generate corrective recovery data during off-nominal contact, the manipulator risks jamming whenever workpiece dimensions deviate by even a millimeter.
4. In **exploratory collection**, an active neural policy or reinforcement learning agent selects actions to maximize an information-theoretic objective, such as epistemic entropy or intrinsic curiosity. Although data throughput matches the robot's peak policy cadence ($50\text{--}100\text{ Hz}$), unconstrained exploratory actions risk high-energy collisions, tripping hardware safety tripwires or degrading mechanical gearboxes through repeated high-torque shock loads.
5. In **autonomous deployment logging**, production policies control actuators during routine factory or warehouse operation, streaming multimodal telemetry into local circular buffers in situ. This channel yields zero-marginal-labor data at the system's full execution rate ($10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ for high-level policies, $1\text{ kHz}$ for joint servos). However, runtime safety barriers heavily censor the recorded state distribution, capturing almost exclusively nominal operating regimes while excluding boundary failures.
6. In **robot-free demonstration**, the operator carries a hand-held gripper fitted with a wrist camera and performs tasks directly in the physical environment, as in the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) [@chi2024umi]. Collection incurs zero robot operating hours or actuator wear, allowing a single demonstrator to gather data across locations where no robot is deployed. The engineering cost shifts to label synthesis: because the hand-held rig records its own Cartesian trajectory and visual feed without robot joint states, actions must be expressed relative to the gripper's pose frame and executed downstream through the target robot's controller. Furthermore, the deployed robot's observation and actuation latencies must be calibrated to match the recording timing (@sec-data-multimodal-time-sync).

[^fn-goertz-force-teleop]: **Bilateral Telemanipulation**\index{Raymond Goertz!bilateral telemanipulation}: Raymond Goertz's 1949 master-slave manipulator at Argonne National Laboratory moved tongs behind radiation shielding in exact correspondence with a master handle, and its mechanical linkage returned the forces at the tongs to the operator's hand [@goertz1949master; @hokayem2006bilateral]. Remote manipulation therefore began with contact force inside the loop. A demonstration recorded through an interface that drops that force channel cannot contain the contact corrections the operator would have made by feel.

A seventh source removes physical hardware entirely. Simulation pipelines eliminate mechanical wear by substituting a numerical contact model for the physical plant, generating synthetic demonstrations at scale. Trajectory generators can expand a few hundred human seed demonstrations across novel object poses and scene layouts, replaying them in physics engines to synthesize tens of thousands of varied trajectories [@mandlekar2023mimicgen]. Downstream policies can then co-train on simulated and real telemetry at a specified mixing ratio. However, these synthetic streams require rigorous metadata tagging: records must log their source generator, physics engine build, integrator step size, and contact solver parameters. Furthermore, the dataset's scenario ledger, the list of required operating conditions that @sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability-geometry builds, must flag every condition covered solely by synthetic rollouts, ensuring that training diagnostics can isolate simulation artifacts from measured physical plant behavior. The provenance requirements for synthetic telemetry appear under dataset degradation (@sec-data-sim-to-real-artifacts).

Because the ingestion source determines how the machine interacts with its physical environment, these data streams occupy disjoint state-action manifolds even when executing identical manipulation tasks. Consider releasing the warehouse mobile manipulator's cage-door latch. A colocated demonstrator guiding the arm feels the latch bind through direct tactile resistance and immediately modulates wrist compliance. A remote teleoperator viewing compressed video streams lacks haptic feedback and exhibits step-and-wait hunting, pausing frequently to verify strike plate contact. A scripted controller advances along a fixed geometric path at constant velocity, producing an identical, rigid contact force spike on every repetition. An exploratory policy approaches at oblique angles, binding the latch until safety tripwires abort the trial. Far from representing noisy variations of a single ground-truth trajectory, these recorded streams reflect distinct dynamical systems characterized by divergent bandwidths, transport latencies, and mechanical compliance profiles, as systematized in @tbl-05-sources-taxonomy.

| Physical Data Source                     | Ingestion Bandwidth & Cadence                                                    | Contact Compliance & Force Awareness                     | Scaling Labor Economics                                     | Collection Boundary Conditions to Check                              |
|:-----------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Kinesthetic teaching**                 | Controller rate; motion bandwidth set by the human arm                           | High (direct physical feel of binding and compliance)    | Very high ($1:1$ dedicated human demonstrator)              | Human contact with links; qualified force and speed limits                |
| **Teleoperation (bilateral/isomorphic)** | Moderate ($20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$, network + human latency)                    | Moderate to high (depends on haptic force feedback)      | High ($1:1$ human operator per active cell)                 | Bounded delay and visibility; isolation and qualified response        |
| **Scripted primitives**                  | High ($50\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$, deterministic trajectory generators)           | Low (rigid trajectories unless impedance-governed)       | Low (automated once authored; engineering upfront)          | Fixture mismatch and contact; guarded trajectory     |
| **Exploratory policy**                   | High ($50\text{--}100\text{ Hz}$, active neural exploration)                     | Variable (learned or randomized contact behaviors)       | Very low (fully autonomous hardware execution)              | Bounded exploration; qualified containment |
| **Autonomous deployment logging**        | Full system rate ($10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ policy, $1\text{ kHz}$ joint servos) | Operational (reflects live deployed closed-loop control) | Zero marginal labor (harvested passively during production) | Qualified operating domain and runtime enforcement            |
| **Robot-free hand-held device**          | Device camera and pose rate; no robot joint stream                               | High (operator feels real contact through the device)    | Moderate (one person per device; no robot time or wear)     | No robot actuation during capture; target execution separately qualified         |
| **Synthetic generation**                 | Simulator step rate, limited by compute                                          | Modeled (contact set by engine and parameters)           | Low after seed demonstrations are recorded                  | No physical actuation during generation; model fidelity and target qualification      |

: **Systems trade-offs across physical demonstration and telemetry sources**: Seven collection sources compared across control dynamics, contact awareness, human labor economics, and the boundary conditions that collection must satisfy. {#tbl-05-sources-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[20,20,20,20,20]"}

```{python}
#| label: calc-data-effective-sample-size
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EFFECTIVE SAMPLE SIZE OF CORRELATED TELEMETRY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-data-collection-sources (effective sample size paragraph)
# │ Goal:    Show how few independent observations one hour of 1 kHz logging
# │          holds when adjacent records are almost perfectly correlated.
# │ Show:    Records per hour; lag-1 correlation; effective sample size.
# │ How:     N = rate * 1 h; N_eff = N (1 - rho) / (1 + rho) for an AR(1)
# │          statistic (Thiebaux and Zwiers 1984).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_sci, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class EffectiveSampleSize:
    """Effective sample size of one hour of permission-tick telemetry."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_log = RM.permission_rate  # one record per permission tick; category: datasheet
    t_log = 1.0 * hour  # category: chosen
    rho = 0.999  # lag-1 autocorrelation of a slowly varying statistic; category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_records = (f_log * t_log).to("").magnitude
    n_eff = n_records * (1.0 - rho) / (1.0 + rho)
    ratio = n_records / n_eff

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(n_records - 3.6e6) < 1e-6, "One hour at 1 kHz should be 3.6 million records")
    check(1790 < n_eff < 1810, "Effective sample size should be about 1,800")
    check(1000 < ratio < 10000, "Step count should overstate independent samples by three orders of magnitude")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_log_str = fmt_frequency(f_log, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)
    n_records_str = fmt_sci(n_records, precision=1)
    rho_str = fmt(rho, precision=3)
    n_eff_str = fmt_int(round(n_eff, -2))
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency((1 / f_log).to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

The cheapest sources in @tbl-05-sources-taxonomy also produce the highest volume of records. This abundance frequently invites a misconception borrowed from disembodied machine learning, where empirical scaling laws correlate model capability directly with raw token count or pretraining dataset volume ($\RawRecordCount$). In physical telemetry, treating every logged control step as an independent observation is a fundamental category error. An edge logger sampling at `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.f_log_str` records `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.n_records_str` state-action pairs every hour, yet adjacent timesteps exhibit near-total temporal autocorrelation ($\SerialAutocorrelation \to 1.0$). Successive kinematic readings sampled `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.t_tick_str` apart differ only by sub-millimeter structural displacements and sensor quantization noise. For a stationary scalar telemetry statistic with geometrically decaying autocorrelation $\SerialAutocorrelation_k = \SerialAutocorrelation^\AutocorrelationLagIndex$, as characterized by a first-order autoregressive AR(1) process, the large-sample *effective sample size* (ESS)[^fn-ess-correlated-telemetry] for estimating its mean is:
$$\EffectiveSampleSize = \RawRecordCount \frac{1 - \SerialAutocorrelation}{1 + \SerialAutocorrelation}.$$ {#eq-data-effective-sample-size}
Under this autoregressive model, an autocorrelation of $\SerialAutocorrelation =$ `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.rho_str` across `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.n_records_str` raw records yields only `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.n_eff_str` statistically independent observations.

While lag-1 correlation alone does not govern ESS across every non-stationary telemetry stream, high-frequency sampling still cannot substitute for operational diversity. In language modeling, consecutive tokens represent high-entropy semantic transitions across an extensive vocabulary. High-rate telemetry can resolve fast contact transients even when the slowly varying statistic used in the ESS example changes little. Increasing its sampling rate does not populate an unvisited scenario cell. Physical dataset coverage expands through independent physical episodes, diverse workpiece placements, varying illumination, and shifting friction coefficients, and never through the clock frequency of the logger. A curated archive containing several hundred episodes that systematically sweep initial geometric and mechanical conditions provides far richer empirical support than millions of repetitive timesteps collected across a static test bench.

[^fn-ess-correlated-telemetry]: **Effective Sample Size**\index{Effective sample size!serially correlated telemetry}: The factor $(1-\SerialAutocorrelation)/(1+\SerialAutocorrelation)$ is the effective-sample-size correction for the mean of a first-order autoregressive series, the correction climatologists apply to serially correlated weather records before testing a trend [@thiebaux1984interpretation]. At the correlation used here it turns an hour of permission-tick records into about `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.n_eff_str` independent ones, so a step count overstates the independent information available for estimating this statistic’s mean by three orders of magnitude before coverage is even considered.

### Human demonstration idiosyncrasies and mechanical artifacts {#sec-data-human-idiosyncrasies}

Because a human operator executes the motions in teleoperated demonstrations, the resulting telemetry permanently embeds the demonstrator's biomechanical limitations, motor recruitment patterns, and perceptual latencies into the training dataset:

- **Neuromuscular sub-movements and physiological tremor:** Human motor control operates through discrete motor unit recruitment bursts rather than continuous, smooth trajectories. These neuromuscular dynamics introduce corrective sub-movements at $2\text{--}3\text{ Hz}$ overlaid with involuntary physiological tremor at $8\text{--}12\text{ Hz}$. If a high-frequency behavioral cloning policy trains on raw joint velocities without low-pass filtering, the neural network imitates this biological tremor as high-frequency torque chatter, accelerating mechanical fatigue in the robot's harmonic drives and gearboxes.
- **Visual latency and step-and-wait hunting:** When an operator guides a manipulator toward a contact fixture using 2D camera monitors, monocular depth ambiguity and video compression latency force an unnatural *step-and-wait* hunting cycle. The operator inches the gripper forward by a few millimeters, pauses for $200\text{--}400\text{ ms}$ to visually confirm clearance or contact across the video stream, and only then resumes motion. An imitation policy trained on uncurated velocity streams treats these latency-induced pauses as deliberate actions, yielding deployed behaviors that stutter, oscillate, or stall mid-trajectory.
- **Attentional narrowing and gaze-conditioned bias:** Human demonstrators naturally focus visual attention on the active tool center point (TCP). Because the operator rarely tracks the peripheral links of the arm during fine manipulation, the robot's elbow or shoulder links frequently sweep perilously close to structural supports or table edges. An imitation policy trained on these demonstrations inherits trajectories that graze workspace obstacles, yet lacks the human's peripheral situational awareness or rapid collision avoidance reflexes.

Because an ingestion logger records every physical tremor, visual hesitation, and marginal joint clearance as an intended demonstration, imitation policies reproduce these operational flaws unless the training pipeline explicitly filters or abstracts them. Selecting a physical telemetry source dictates what raw experience reaches the archive; formulating the corresponding action labels dictates what control dynamics the policy extracts from that experience.

## Action Label Selection and Supervisory Grounding {#sec-data-action-label}

By the time the gripper contacts the strike plate on the cage-door latch, the operator's input motion has transformed into four distinct numerical signals across the system hierarchy. Which signal the ingestion pipeline designates as the supervisory target determines what behavioral dynamics the neural policy internalizes. The robot splits its computational architecture across two decoupled processing domains:

- The unprivileged **Linux application processor** executes perception pipelines, handles video frame ingestion, runs teleoperation input mapping, and computes the neural policy forward pass ($\Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t})$).
- On the permission side of the proposal boundary, a hard real-time **safety microcontroller (MCU)** runs joint and permission checks at the chosen `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.f_log_str` cadence. Dedicated motor-drive logic closes the faster field-oriented current loop; its current samples remain distinct from the telemetry retained at each permission tick.[^fn-capture-encoder-dma]

[^fn-capture-encoder-dma]: **Hardware Input Capture**\index{Input capture!DMA latching}: On real-time MCUs, a timer's input-capture unit latches encoder counts and current-shunt conversions at a hardware edge, and Direct Memory Access (DMA) moves them to memory without waiting on software. Sampling jitter stays within microseconds, so the denominator of a numerically differentiated velocity or acceleration carries no scheduling noise.

### The four-stream action tap tuple {#sec-data-four-stream-action-tap}

A command can be logged at each of the four causal stages it passes through, and the **four-stream action tap**\index{Four-stream action tap!definition}\index{Action tap!definition} $(\RequestedActionTap, \MappedCommandTap, \EnforcedCommandTap, \MeasuredResponseTap)$ is the tuple that records all four, two on each side of the boundary between the unprivileged Linux host and the discrete safety MCU (@fig-05-action-taps). Tap 1 ($\RequestedActionTap$) captures raw policy or operator intent before kinematic mapping; Tap 2 ($\MappedCommandTap$) logs the mapped command prior to the black-channel link; Tap 3 ($\EnforcedCommandTap$) captures the admitted command following the 1 kHz permission check; and Tap 4 ($\MeasuredResponseTap$) records the physical plant response measured by joint encoders and current shunts. All four streams converge into a hardware-synchronized telemetry log, ensuring that interventions and tracking errors remain fully auditable.

::: {#fig-05-action-taps fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Four-stream action tap tuple**: Four places a command can be logged, from raw policy intent on the application processor through to measured plant response. Which tap a dataset records decides what the model learns to imitate. The four-tap decomposition is this book's construct; the teleoperation rigs it instruments follow @zhao2023learning and @wu2023gello." fig-alt="Block diagram. On the application processor, a policy or operator box feeds a kinematic mapping box; tap 1, a req, sits between them and tap 2, a cmd, sits after the mapping. A black-channel link with no shared memory crosses the dashed proposal boundary to the discrete safety MCU, which holds the permission path at a 1 kHz tick. Tap 3, a enf, sits after the permission path, which feeds the drives that close the current loops and apply the torque limit. The drives move the plant, joint encoders measure the motion over an interval, and tap 4, a meas, leaves the encoders. All four taps run down to a synchronized telemetry log stamped with hardware timestamps."}
![](images/svg/fig05_four_stream_action_taps.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Dividing telemetry logging across the unprivileged Linux host and the hard real-time MCU captures four distinct physical semantics:

- **Tap 1: The requested action ($\RequestedActionTap$, "Asked"):** Logged in user space on the application processor, this represents unconstrained human operator input (from a leader arm or joystick) or the raw forward-pass output from an unverified policy, tagged with its native coordinate frame and issue timestamp prior to software validation. This proposal reflects unadulterated human or policy intent, but it frequently demands infeasible joint accelerations or violates spatial bounding envelopes.
- **Tap 2: The mapped command ($\MappedCommandTap$, "Mapped"):** The kinematically retargeted setpoint (such as Cartesian end-effector velocities converted to joint space setpoints via inverse kinematics), incorporating coordinate frame transformations, trajectory interpolation, and workspace limits before transmission across the black-channel board link to the safety MCU.
- **Tap 3: The enforced command ($\EnforcedCommandTap$, "Allowed"):** Logged on the bare-metal MCU on the permission side of the boundary, this represents the command after deterministic Control Barrier Functions (CBFs, safety filters that keep states within a forward-invariant safe set), velocity and acceleration clamps, torque saturation envelopes, and collision guards have checked or modified the proposal. Whichever tap a dataset chooses as its label, the imitation loss has the same form; written for the admitted command, it is:
  $$\PolicyImitationLoss(\ModelParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \EnforcedCommandLabel) \sim \DemonstrationDataset} \left[ \LossFunction(\Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t}), \EnforcedCommandLabel) \right],$$
  Here the training dataset must contain curated, correctly attributed targets. Passing the permission check does not make a command an expert demonstration: a clamp or emergency stop may be a safeguard's response to a poor request. Override flags and companion taps determine which records can serve as imitation targets and which remain evidence of intervention.
- **Tap 4: The measured response ($\MeasuredResponseTap$, "Done"):** The physical plant reaction measured by optical joint encoders and motor current shunt resistors over the executed control tick, recording actual mechanical displacement and electrical effort. This measured response serves as proprioceptive state input ($\NextProprioceptiveObservation$) for subsequent policy steps rather than an action label.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Control barrier functions and the forward-invariant safe sets they enforce are developed in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.
:::

These distinctions become critical when commanded intent and physical motion diverge. If a teleoperator requests an aggressive movement that the safety permission path clamps, the resulting state transition follows the enforced command ($\EnforcedCommandTap$), not the unconstrained request ($\RequestedActionTap$). Pairing that transition only with the request conceals the safety intervention and teaches a policy to repeat demands the physical machine cannot execute.

At the latch, the opposite ambiguity arises. Contact resistance can bring measured joint velocities to zero ($\MeasuredJointVelocities \approx \ZeroVector$) while the motors continue exerting holding torque against the strike plate. Treating that response as a deliberate zero-velocity target loses the distinction between maintaining effort against the latch and choosing to stop. The appropriate imitation target depends on the policy's action interface; the other taps explain how that target became physical motion.

Retaining all four streams is what makes any single choice of label interpretable. A policy trained on the request alone learns commands the permission path would have clamped, and one trained on the measured response alone learns the arm's compliance, backlash, and external disturbances as if they were intended control. A log that keeps only the final encoder state or only the operator's input discards exactly the stages at which software and safety hardware changed the command. The tuple is also only as reliable as its shared clock. The application processor and the MCU must stamp their taps in one hardware-synchronized timebase, such as the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP), written $\PtpHardwareTimestamp$, because a few milliseconds of skew between them misaligns each visual observation from the torque it prompted (@sec-data-multimodal-time-sync).

For the latch campaign, the imitation target is the mapped command whenever it represents an expert request that the permission path accepted unchanged. In that case $\MappedCommandTap$ and $\EnforcedCommandTap$ carry the same value, so the choice between the two taps matters only for commands the permission path modified. A modified command remains a separate, attributed intervention; a curated recovery can later supply an expert target at that state. Each training pair therefore carries two times. The observation is dated when its physics was true, at the exposure midpoint, and the command is dated when the operator issued it. The gap between them is part of the demonstration and is recorded rather than erased, because it contains the operator's own reaction time (@sec-data-bilateral-passivity). The alignment developed below supplies the first of these times.

### Multi-modal time synchronization and exposure midpoint alignment {#sec-data-multimodal-time-sync}

Recording the right action tap does not settle when each recorded value was physically true. In embodied platforms, sensory modalities operate at widely different sampling cadences and physical propagation regimes: cameras integrate photons over exposure windows of $10\text{--}35\text{ ms}$ at $30\text{--}60\text{ Hz}$, 6-axis force-torque sensors stream over a Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) or Controller Area Network (CAN) bus at $100\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$, joint and permission telemetry is retained at the MCU's chosen $1\text{ kHz}$ tick while motor-drive current sampling serves the faster local current loop, and neural policy models dispatch setpoints at $10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$. A naive data loader that simply latches the latest available sensor sample pairs each action with a camera frame whose exposure was centered $25\text{--}40\text{ ms}$ before the frame arrived in host memory, and it records that frame as the present state. The resulting policy learns to map historical visual states to present actions, baking artificial phase lag directly into its weights. This timing error belongs to the logging pipeline, not to the demonstration, so correct timestamps let the pairing process account for it.

```{python}
#| label: calc-data-sync-displacement
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OBSERVATION-ACTION SYNC DISPLACEMENT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-data-multimodal-time-sync
# │ Goal:    Compare the displacement an uncompensated observation-action lag
# │          injects against the latch clearance, at transit and latch speeds.
# │ Show:    Displacement at 0.50 m/s transit and at the two latch approaches;
# │          the largest tolerable lag at each latch speed.
# │ How:     dx = v * lag; lag_max = clearance / v. Latch speeds from AISLE;
# │          transit speed, lag, and clearance are chapter-local scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_multiple, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class SyncDisplacement:
    """Displacement from pairing an observation with an action across a lag."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_transit = 0.50 * meter / second  # generic arm transit speed; category: illustrative
    t_lag = 35.0 * millisecond  # uncompensated exposure-to-arrival lag; category: illustrative
    clearance = 2.0 * millimeter  # latch clearance; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    v_guarded = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: illustrative
    v_fast = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative
    t_skew_lo = 15.0 * millisecond  # full-frame rolling-shutter skew, fast readout; category: illustrative
    t_skew_hi = 33.0 * millisecond  # full-frame rolling-shutter skew, one 30 Hz frame; category: illustrative
    clearance_tight = 1.0 * millimeter  # tighter strike plate asked about in the checkpoint; category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dx_transit = (v_transit * t_lag).to(millimeter)
    dx_guarded = (v_guarded * t_lag).to(millimeter)
    dx_fast = (v_fast * t_lag).to(millimeter)
    transit_over_clearance = (dx_transit / clearance).to("").magnitude
    lag_max_guarded = (clearance / v_guarded).to(millisecond)
    lag_max_fast = (clearance / v_fast).to(millisecond)
    dx_skew_transit = (v_transit * t_skew_hi).to(millimeter)
    dx_skew_fast = (v_fast * t_skew_hi).to(millimeter)
    lag_max_tight = (clearance_tight / v_fast).to(millisecond)  # checkpoint answer; not printed

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dx_transit.magnitude - 17.5) < 1e-9, "Transit displacement should be 17.5 mm")
    check(dx_guarded < clearance, "The guarded approach should fit the clearance at this lag")
    check(dx_fast > clearance, "The faster approach should exceed the clearance at this lag")
    check(abs(lag_max_fast.magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, "Largest tolerable lag at 0.10 m/s should be 20 ms")
    check(dx_skew_fast > clearance, "Worst-case rolling-shutter skew at 0.10 m/s should exceed the clearance")
    check(lag_max_tight < t_lag, "The checkpoint's tighter plate should reject the uncompensated lag at the faster approach")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_transit_str = fmt_velocity(v_transit, precision=2)
    t_lag_str = fmt_latency(t_lag, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    clearance_str = fmt_length(clearance, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    v_guarded_str = fmt_velocity(v_guarded, precision=2)
    v_fast_str = fmt_velocity(v_fast, precision=2)
    dx_transit_str = fmt_length(dx_transit, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    dx_guarded_str = fmt_length(dx_guarded, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    dx_fast_str = fmt_length(dx_fast, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    transit_over_clearance_mult_str = fmt_multiple(transit_over_clearance, precision=1)
    lag_max_guarded_str = fmt_latency(lag_max_guarded, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    lag_max_fast_str = fmt_latency(lag_max_fast, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_skew_lo_str = fmt_latency(t_skew_lo, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_skew_hi_str = fmt_latency(t_skew_hi, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dx_skew_transit_str = fmt_length(dx_skew_transit, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    dx_skew_fast_str = fmt_length(dx_skew_fast, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    clearance_tight_str = fmt_length(clearance_tight, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

To quantify the physical hazard of temporal misalignment, consider the spatial tracking error $\SyncPairingDisplacement$ injected into the dataset when an observation and an action are paired across an uncompensated phase lag $\ObservationPairingLag$:
$$\SyncPairingDisplacement(\TimeInstant) = \int_{t - \ObservationPairingLag}^{\TimeInstant} \Velocity(\IntegrationDummyTime)\,d\IntegrationDummyTime \approx \Velocity(\TimeInstant) \cdot \ObservationPairingLag.$$ {#eq-data-sync-displacement}
The latch campaign moves far more slowly than an arm in transit, and notebook \ref{nbk-data-pairing-lag} applies @eq-data-sync-displacement at both speeds.

::: {#nbk-data-pairing-lag .callout-notebook title="The pairing lag"}

**Problem**: A logger pairs each action with a camera frame whose exposure midpoint lies an uncompensated `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` earlier. Does the resulting pairing error fit the `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` latch clearance at transit speed and at the latch campaign's two approach speeds, and how much lag can each approach tolerate?

**Variables**:

- Uncompensated lag $\ObservationPairingLag =$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` (illustrative; exposure-to-arrival delay of an untimed logger)
- Latch clearance $\LatchClearance =$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` (illustrative)
- Transit speed `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_transit_str` (illustrative); guarded approach `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str` and faster approach `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` (illustrative scenario speeds of the running machine)

**Math**:

1. **Transit**: `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_transit_str` $\times$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_transit_str`, `{python} SyncDisplacement.transit_over_clearance_mult_str` the clearance.
2. **Guarded approach**: `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str` $\times$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_guarded_str`, inside the clearance.
3. **Faster approach**: `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` $\times$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_fast_str`, outside it.
4. **Lag ceilings**: $\PairingLagCeiling = \LatchClearance/\ApproachSpeed$, so `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` $/$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_guarded_str` and `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` $/$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_fast_str`.

**Result**: The same lag fits the modeled pairing-error allocation at the guarded approach and exceeds it at the faster one.

**Systems insight**: A timing error becomes a position error at the speed of the motion, just as observation age becomes blind travel $\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay$ in the stopping budget derived in @sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake. The faster approach cannot be collected without the exposure-midpoint alignment of the four-stage pipeline in @sec-data-alignment-pipeline.

:::

When an imitation learning model trains on misaligned pairs, it fits a relationship in which the action appears to precede the visual evidence that prompted it. During closed-loop deployment, that artificial phase lag appears as overshoot, control hunting, and chattering against rigid surfaces. Because displacement grows linearly with lag, each approach speed has a lag ceiling equal to the clearance divided by the speed, and @fig-05-sync-displacement places those ceilings beside a second timing error the notebook did not count. A full-frame rolling-shutter skew of `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_lo_str` to `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_hi_str` is comparable to the uncompensated lag, so a logger that stamps every frame correctly can still breach the faster approach's `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_fast_str` ceiling through readout alone.

::: {#fig-05-sync-displacement fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**One lag, three verdicts**: Pairing an observation with an action across an uncompensated lag displaces the recorded state by speed times lag. At `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` the transit pairing is `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_transit_str` off, the faster latch approach exceeds the `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` clearance, and the guarded approach stays inside it. The clearance tolerates at most `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_fast_str` of lag at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` and `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_guarded_str` at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str`; a full-frame rolling-shutter skew alone spans `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_lo_str` to `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_hi_str`." fig-alt="Log-log plot of pairing displacement in millimeters against observation-to-action lag in milliseconds, 1 to 100 ms. Three straight parallel lines: transit at 0.50 meters per second on top, the faster latch approach at 0.10 meters per second, and the guarded approach at 0.03 meters per second at the bottom. A red dashed horizontal line marks the 2 millimeter latch clearance. A dotted vertical line at 35 ms marks the uncompensated lag, with a dot on each line. Red squares where the latch lines cross the clearance are labeled at most 20 ms and at most 66.7 ms. A gray band from 15 to 33 ms marks full-frame rolling-shutter skew."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-05-sync-displacement
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OBSERVATION-ACTION LAG AGAINST THE LATCH CLEARANCE (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-05-sync-displacement in @sec-data-multimodal-time-sync,
# │          after calc-data-sync-displacement.
# │ Goal:    Show that the same pairing lag is harmless at the guarded approach
# │          and disqualifying at the faster one.
# │ Show:    dx = v * lag for the transit and both latch speeds; the latch
# │          clearance; the 35 ms uncompensated lag; each speed's largest
# │          tolerable lag; the full-frame rolling-shutter skew band.
# │ How:     Every value reads SyncDisplacement (no literals).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check

S = SyncDisplacement
ms = lambda q: q.to(millisecond).magnitude
mm = lambda q: q.to(millimeter).magnitude
mmps = lambda q: q.to(millimeter / millisecond).magnitude
c = mm(S.clearance)
lag = ms(S.t_lag)
lines = [  # label, speed, role color
    (f"transit {S.v_transit_str}", mmps(S.v_transit), "#4A5568"),
    (f"faster latch approach {S.v_fast_str}", mmps(S.v_fast), "#B87333"),
    (f"guarded latch approach {S.v_guarded_str}", mmps(S.v_guarded), "#007A87"),
]
check(abs(mmps(S.v_transit) * lag - mm(S.dx_transit)) < 1e-9, "transit line matches dx_transit")
check(abs(c / mmps(S.v_fast) - ms(S.lag_max_fast)) < 1e-9, "fast crossing matches lag_max_fast")

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
t = np.geomspace(1, 100, 400)
ax.axvspan(ms(S.t_skew_lo), ms(S.t_skew_hi), color="#A0AEC0", alpha=0.18, lw=0)
ax.text((ms(S.t_skew_lo) * ms(S.t_skew_hi)) ** 0.5, 60, "full-frame\nrolling-shutter skew", fontsize=7.5, color="#4A5568", ha="center", va="top")
ax.axhline(c, color="#A51C30", lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 3)))
ax.text(1.1, c * 1.1, f"latch clearance {S.clearance_str}", fontsize=8, color="#A51C30", ha="left", va="bottom")
ax.axvline(lag, color="#1A202C", lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
ax.text(lag * 1.05, 0.12, f"uncompensated\nlag {S.t_lag_str}", fontsize=7.5, color="#1A202C", va="bottom")
for lab, v, col in lines:
    ax.plot(t, v * t, color=col, lw=1.8)
    ax.plot(lag, v * lag, "o", color=col, ms=5, zorder=5)
    ax.text(105, v * 100, lab, fontsize=7.5, color=col, va="center")
for v, lab in ((mmps(S.v_fast), S.lag_max_fast_str), (mmps(S.v_guarded), S.lag_max_guarded_str)):
    tx = c / v
    ax.plot(tx, c, "s", color="#A51C30", ms=4.5, zorder=6)
    ax.text(tx * 1.07, c * 0.86, f"≤ {lab}", fontsize=7.5, color="#A51C30", ha="left", va="top")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1, 100)
ax.set_ylim(0.1, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("observation-to-action pairing lag (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("pairing displacement (mm)")
for s in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```
:::

#### Hardware timestamps vs. software arrival timestamps {#sec-data-hw-vs-sw-timestamps}

The root of temporal corruption lies in conflating when an optical or electrical event occurred in physics with when the operating system kernel noticed it in software:

- **Software arrival timestamps ($\HostArrivalTimestamp$):** In naive logging pipelines, an image frame or CAN packet is timestamped when the Linux kernel handles the device interrupt or when a user-space thread dequeues the buffer from Video4Linux2 (V4L2) or a socket. This host timestamp incorporates camera pixel readout time, USB 3 or MIPI CSI-2 bus serialization, Direct Memory Access (DMA) latency, and operating system scheduling jitter:
  $$\HostArrivalTimestamp = \ExposureMidpointTime + \frac{\ExposureDuration}{2} + \FrameReadoutTime + \BusSerializationTime + \DriverInterruptLatency + \TimestampJitterDelay.$$
  Host timestamps lag physical reality by $20\text{--}45\text{ ms}$. In an untuned system, operating system scheduling jitter ($\TimestampJitterDelay = \pm 5\text{--}15\text{ ms}$), driven by kernel preemption latency, CPU C-state power wake-up transitions, and USB host controller interrupt coalescing (where packets are held in hardware buffers until a threshold count or timer expires), corrupts numerical differentiation. When joint velocities are computed via backward difference:
  $$\GeneralizedVelocities_k = \frac{\GeneralizedCoordinates_k - \GeneralizedCoordinates_{k-1}}{\TimeInstant_k - \TimeInstant_{k-1}},$$
  a nominal $1\text{ kHz}$ sampling interval ($\FiniteChange \TimeInstant = 1.0\text{ ms}$) perturbed by software timestamp jitter $\TimestampJitterDelay = \pm 0.5\text{ ms}$ causes the denominator to fluctuate between $0.5\text{ ms}$ and $1.5\text{ ms}$, doubling the inferred velocity at the shorter interval or reducing it by one third at the longer interval for the same measured displacement. If thread preemption reverses packet dequeuing order ($\TimeInstant_k < \TimeInstant_{k-1}$), the computed velocity reverses sign, injecting spurious velocity spikes into the training targets.
- **Hardware PTP timestamps ($\PtpHardwareTimestamp$):** Hardware timestamps isolate the physical event from host scheduling delays. IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP) estimates clock offset across distributed nodes using a deterministic two-way message exchange.[^fn-ptp-pairing-bias] The reference clock sends at $\TimeInstant_1$ and receives the reply at $\TimeInstant_4$; the remote clock receives at $\TimeInstant_2$ and replies at $\TimeInstant_3$. Under symmetric path delays, the propagation delay and offset are:
  $$\PtpPropagationDelay = \frac{(\TimeInstant_4 - \TimeInstant_1) - (\TimeInstant_3 - \TimeInstant_2)}{2}, \qquad \ClockOffset = \frac{(\TimeInstant_2 - \TimeInstant_1) - (\TimeInstant_4 - \TimeInstant_3)}{2}.$$
  Engineers must treat the symmetric-path assumption with care. Hardware timestamping bounds uncertainty, but a network packet timestamp does not automatically equal an optical exposure midpoint. Production logs must preserve the capture event, clock domain identity, and bounded conversion error. The key collection decision is whether that uncertainty fits within the task's spatial alignment tolerance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Protocol:** The IEEE 1588 message exchange, its clock servo, and its path-asymmetry uncertainty are developed in @sec-appendix-systems-ptp.
:::

[^fn-ptp-pairing-bias]: **Precision Time Protocol (PTP)**\index{IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol!pairing error}: IEEE 1588 was first published in 2002 for test-and-measurement and industrial-automation networks, and its current revision dates from 2019 [@ieee15882019]. It reaches sub-microsecond agreement only when both endpoints timestamp packets in hardware at the network interface. Its weak point is the symmetric-path assumption in the offset formula, because a link whose two directions differ in delay biases the computed offset by half that difference, and every observation-action pairing in the archive inherits the bias.

#### Rolling shutter skew across camera streams {#sec-data-rolling-shutter-skew}

A severe and frequently overlooked visual artifact in physical AI pipelines is **rolling shutter skew**. Low-cost consumer sensors and webcams expose pixel rows sequentially rather than instantaneously. For a sensor with $\ImageHeight$ vertical scanlines and line readout duration $\RollingShutterRowReadout$, row $\SensorRowIndex \in [0, \ImageHeight-1]$ begins its exposure at $\RowExposureStartTime(\SensorRowIndex)$, and its exposure midpoint, half an exposure later, depends linearly on its vertical coordinate:
$$\RowExposureStartTime(\SensorRowIndex) + \frac{\ExposureDuration}{2} = \ExposureStartTime + \SensorRowIndex \, \RollingShutterRowReadout + \frac{\ExposureDuration}{2}.$$
Across a full frame, the temporal skew between the top row ($\SensorRowIndex = 0$) and bottom row ($\SensorRowIndex = \ImageHeight - 1$) accumulates to:
$$\RollingShutterFrameSkew = (\ImageHeight - 1) \, \RollingShutterRowReadout,$$ {#eq-data-rolling-shutter-skew}
which for common sensors lies between about `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_lo_str` and `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_hi_str`, the upper end being one full frame period at 30 Hz. When the robot arm or camera moves at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_transit_str`, the bottom of the manipulator in the image is captured while the physical link has moved up to `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_skew_transit_str` relative to the top of the link in the same frame. Even at the faster latch approach of `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str`, the worst-case skew moves the gripper `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_skew_fast_str` within one frame, exceeding the `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` clearance. This geometric warping (the "jello effect") deforms straight edges into curved arcs and breaks rigid-body geometry.

Independent rolling shutters can depict the same moving arm at different poses within nominally simultaneous frames. Hardware-triggered global shutters simplify alignment; rolling shutters require a row-time model and a motion bound or correction. Sensor choice must follow the task tolerance rather than an unyielding demand for a single shutter architecture.

#### A four-stage alignment pipeline {#sec-data-alignment-pipeline}

Hardware timestamps fix when each sample was taken, and the row-time model fixes when each part of an image was exposed. A collection pipeline still has to turn those facts into training pairs whose pairing error fits inside the clearance budget of notebook \ref{nbk-data-pairing-lag}. It can implement that alignment contract in four stages:

1. **Hardware-triggered optical exposure midpoint:** The real-time MCU dispatches hardware GPIO sync pulses or PTP-synchronized trigger packets to every triggerable camera. The rig mixes shutter types: the wrist camera's global shutter exposes all rows together, while the navigation camera and the external cameras' color sensors read out row by row, so their frames also need the row-time model above to assign each row its own midpoint. The camera latches the trigger at $\ExposureStartTime$, and the driver calculates the true optical midpoint $\ExposureMidpointTime = \ExposureStartTime + \ExposureDuration / 2$ in hardware PTP clock units ($\PtpHardwareTimestamp$), avoiding host arrival time as the exposure timestamp.[^fn-trigger-camera-exposure]
2. **Lock-free time-sorted jitter compensation:** Because network and bus transfers exhibit variable transport delay $\TimestampJitterDelay$, incoming sensor packets are stamped with their hardware PTP capture timestamp and inserted into a lock-free, time-sorted jitter ring buffer in shared memory. An asynchronous consumer thread advances a playhead lagging real-time by a fixed, bounded window ($\JitterBufferPlayoutDelay = 15\text{--}25\text{ ms}$), absorbing transport bursts and re-ordering packets into monotonic hardware timestamp sequence.
3. **Cubic Hermite kinematic interpolation:** Because joint encoders sample at $1\text{ kHz}$ ($1\text{ ms}$ period) while cameras capture at $30\text{ Hz}$ or $60\text{ Hz}$, the camera midpoint $\ExposureMidpointTime$ falls between two discrete MCU telemetry ticks $\TimeInstant_k$ and $\TimeInstant_{k+1}$. The synchronization thread interpolates joint angles $\GeneralizedCoordinates(\ExposureMidpointTime)$ using cubic Hermite splines across the bounding kinematic records $(\TimeInstant_k, \GeneralizedCoordinates_k, \GeneralizedVelocities_k)$ and $(\TimeInstant_{k+1}, \GeneralizedCoordinates_{k+1}, \GeneralizedVelocities_{k+1})$:
   $$\GeneralizedCoordinates(\ExposureMidpointTime) = \HermiteBasisFunction_{00}(\HermiteInterpolationFraction) \GeneralizedCoordinates_k + \HermiteBasisFunction_{10}(\HermiteInterpolationFraction) \TelemetryTickInterval \GeneralizedVelocities_k + \HermiteBasisFunction_{01}(\HermiteInterpolationFraction) \GeneralizedCoordinates_{k+1} + \HermiteBasisFunction_{11}(\HermiteInterpolationFraction) \TelemetryTickInterval \GeneralizedVelocities_{k+1},$$
   where $\TelemetryTickInterval = \TimeInstant_{k+1} - \TimeInstant_k = 1\text{ ms}$, $\HermiteInterpolationFraction = (\ExposureMidpointTime - \TimeInstant_k)/\TelemetryTickInterval \in [0, 1]$ is the fraction of the tick elapsed at the exposure midpoint, and $\HermiteBasisFunction_{ij}(\HermiteInterpolationFraction)$ are the cubic Hermite basis functions (@sec-appendix-control-splines). This gives a smooth state estimate between valid samples. The interpolation error still needs a bound, especially across contact or missing telemetry.
4. **Pre-serialization alignment:** Container formats store multi-rate topics with the timestamps provided by the logger. Alignment may occur during capture or in a versioned preprocessing pass. Preserve the raw timestamps and interpolation provenance in either case, so the training pair carries an estimated state and its uncertainty rather than an assertion of exact simultaneity.
